title: Pattern classification in line plots: effects of data complexity and individual differences in cognition
abstract: Abstract Understanding how people interpret visual patterns is central to theories of visual cognition and the design of effective visualizations. In this work, we investigate pattern classification performance in line-plot visualizations as a function of visual complexity, individual cognitive traits, and their interaction. Visual complexity is operationalized using information-theoretic measures of section-level and contextual entropy, while individual differences are captured through measures of cognitive style, relational complexity, and field independence/dependence. We report results from a controlled web-based experiment with 282 participants who classified local patterns in line plots following a brief training phase. Performance was analyzed using a Bayesian generalized linear mixed-effects model. The results show that visual complexity exerts systematic but non-uniform effects on classification accuracy. Section-level entropy is generally associated with decreased performance, whereas contextual entropy exhibits a more nuanced role. Critically, these effects are moderated by individual cognitive traits. In particular, experiential processing and relational complexity show asymmetric interactions with visual entropy, indicating that cognitive abilities primarily modulate sensitivity to different forms of visual complexity rather than uniformly improving performance. These findings suggest that visual pattern classification emerges from the interaction between perceptual processing demands and individual cognitive characteristics.
